The KV-Surgeon: Compensation-Aware Offline KV-Cache Compaction

Moritz Wagner ††thanks: Correspondence to: Moritz Wagner wagner@zib.de Affiliation: Department for AI in Society, Science, and Technology, Zuse Institute Berlin, Germany    Christophe Roux    Max Zimmer    Sebastian Pokutta Affiliation: Institute of Mathematics, Technische Universität Berlin, Germany
Abstract

Offline compaction of the key–value cache (KV-cache) reduces the cost of repeatedly querying a fixed context by constructing a smaller cache once and reusing it subsequently. The central challenge of compaction is deciding which cache entries to delete and which to retain. Existing methods score each candidate for deletion on its own, with the rest of the cache being held fixed. However, softmax renormalization of the attention operation couples these decisions in a nonlinear manner: removing one entry changes the attention weights of every remaining one. In this work, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses calibration data to take interactions into account in a tractable way. We derive a quadratic surrogate that admits closed-form expressions for jointly making the optimal greedy removal decision as well as compensation within the remaining entries. On QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, and at every evaluated compaction ratio, KV-Surgeon substantially advances the cost–accuracy Pareto frontier of dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters. At 50×50\times compaction, KV-Surgeon improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), the state of the art, at comparable cost. Lastly, we introduce an even faster variant, which also exceeds the state of the art while requiring only two fifths of its cost.

1 Introduction

Many large language model (LLM) applications repeatedly query a fixed context such as a document, patient record, or codebase. The key–value cache (KV-cache) for such a context grows linearly with its length and occupies a large fraction of the memory used during long-context inference. Every attention layer reads this cache for every generated token, so every request pays for its size in both memory and latency. Offline compaction reduces this cost by processing the context once and compressing the resulting cache, which is then used to serve all later requests (Eyuboglu et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Zweiger et al., 2026).

Unlike serving-time eviction, which discards cache entries within the forward pass of a request (Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024), offline compaction can spend a larger one-time budget that is amortized over future requests. In particular, it can use calibration queries, i.e., query vectors the model produces while re-reading or discussing the context, to decide which entries to retain. Eyuboglu et al. (2026) introduce this regime with Cartridges, which trains a new latent cache per context. More recent work makes offline compaction much cheaper by replacing end-to-end training with eviction-inspired selection and efficient optimization of the remaining cache (Zweiger et al., 2026).

The central problem in cache compaction is deciding which cache entries can be removed while preserving the resulting attention outputs. For one attention head, a cache of TT entries contains a key kj∈ℝdkk_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} and a value vj∈ℝdvv_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} at each position j=1,…,Tj=1,\ldots,T. A query q∈ℝdkq\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} produces

P≜softmax⁡((q⊤​kℓdk)ℓ=1T)∈ℝT,o≜∑j=1TPj​vj∈ℝdv,P\triangleq\operatorname{softmax}\left(\left(\frac{q^{\top}k_{\ell}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)_{\ell=1}^{T}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{T},\qquad o\triangleq\sum_{j=1}^{T}P_{j}v_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}},

where PjP_{j} is the attention weight of entry jj and oo is the resulting output. Removing cache entry jj does not simply subtract Pj​vjP_{j}v_{j}, since softmax renormalization changes the attention weights of all remaining entries. The effect of one deletion therefore depends on which other entries remain, making selection a combinatorial problem rather than a ranking problem. Scores based only on received attention, as in attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), additionally overlook value redundancy: if an entry’s value is close to the output the head already produces, i.e., ∥vj−o∥22\lVert v_{j}-o\rVert_{2}^{2} is small, removing it might change the output little, even when its attention weight is large. Good selection must therefore account not only for the contribution of each entry, but also for how deletions interact.

Recent output-aware methods instead estimate the output error caused by deleting a single entry (Goel et al., 2026; An et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026). CAOTE (Goel et al., 2026) derives the exact change caused by deleting one entry for a single calibration query, and OBCache (Gu et al., 2026) uses a Taylor approximation of the attention output error aggregated across queries. These methods nevertheless evaluate the deletion of one entry while the rest of the cache is held fixed. Attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026) refits the retained cache to minimize the error of the compacted output, but only after the retained set has been chosen. What is missing is compensation-aware selection: each candidate deletion should be scored by the error remaining after the surviving entries have been adjusted to compensate for it, so that selection and refitting are optimized jointly rather than in sequence. This is difficult under softmax attention because deletion changes the normalization itself, so the error after both deletion and compensation has no obvious closed form.

In this work, we substantially advance the cost–accuracy Pareto frontier for offline KV-cache compaction. We derive a quadratic surrogate that makes compensation-aware selection tractable. We introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses this surrogate for greedy, compensation-aware elimination. For each candidate deletion, the surrogate admits closed-form expressions for both the optimal compensating update and the resulting increase in surrogate loss. Each candidate entry is assigned a score after the remaining entries have been adjusted to compensate for its removal, and the update is then applied to the cache, so the next deletion is chosen against the compensated entries, as Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) (Hassibi & Stork, 1993) does for network weights.

We evaluate KV-Surgeon on QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, using dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters and compaction ratios from 5×5\times to 100×100\times. Across these settings, KV-Surgeon improves the cost–accuracy frontier at every ratio, achieving higher mean accuracy at comparable cost. Mean question-answering accuracy across our experiments exceeds the state of the art by 4.34.3 percentage points at 100×100\times compaction and 3.03.0 percentage points at 50×50\times. The gains are less pronounced at 5×5\times and 10×10\times, where the strongest methods already suffer almost no deterioration relative to the uncompacted cache. At 50×50\times compaction the state of the art, attention matching with its AM-HAK selection rule (Zweiger et al., 2026), reaches 62.0%62.0\% accuracy in 138138 seconds11 1 Pipeline times differ by more than an order of magnitude between model–benchmark pairs, so an arithmetic mean would be dominated by the slowest pair. We therefore report the geometric mean of the pipeline times. per context. KV-Surgeon reaches 65.1%65.1\% in 145145 seconds, and KV-Surgeon-fast reaches 63.9%63.9\% in 5454 seconds. Figure 1 shows the resulting frontier at 50×50\times compaction on the largest model we evaluate.

Our contributions are the following.

  1. 1.

    Quadratic surrogate. We derive a quadratic surrogate to the exact attention-output error, which allows us to design efficient methods for approximately solving the compaction problem.

  2. 2.

    Compensation-aware selection. Based on this surrogate, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which iteratively removes entries while adjusting the remaining entries in closed form after each deletion, then jointly refits the retained cache. Unlike prior output-aware scores or post-selection refitting, compensation directly influences which entries are retained.

  3. 3.

    A new cost–accuracy Pareto frontier. Across QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters, and 5×5\times to 100×100\times compaction, KV-Surgeon substantially advances the frontier, with gains at every evaluated ratio and the largest improvements at 50×50\times and 100×100\times. We show empirically that accounting for compensation during selection substantially improves accuracy over exact single-deletion scoring.

2 Related work

Other forms of KV-cache compression. KV-caches can be compressed along several axes. Quantization lowers the precision of stored keys and values (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024), and low-rank methods reduce the feature dimension (Saxena et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2025). Both are complementary to reducing the number of entries. A different route, LLM summarization, shortens the text input itself by prompting an LLM to summarize it. This approach transfers across models, but gives no direct control over cache size. We study compaction along the sequence dimension, where a fixed budget of entries is retained from an already computed cache.

Offline compaction. Offline methods exploit contexts that are processed once and queried repeatedly. Cartridges (Eyuboglu et al., 2026) trains a new latent cache per context from self-generated data. KVzip (Kim et al., 2026) removes cache entries based on the attention they receive while the model repeats the context verbatim. Attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026) also keeps a subset of the original keys, then fits a scalar logit bias per retained key and refits the stored values to reproduce the original attention outputs on reference queries. Its AM-HAK variant selects entries by root-mean-square attention, and AM-OMP, based on orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP), greedily selects keys so that their reweighted attention reproduces the attention mass of the full cache. In both, the support is chosen from attention statistics before the values are refit, so the ability of the retained entries to reproduce the output does not influence selection.

Eviction by proxy scores. Serving-time eviction discards entries within a single request, ranking each one by a score that ignores the rest of the cache: accumulated attention, as in H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) and related methods (Oren et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023), or a query-free proxy such as position (Xiao et al., 2024), key norm (Devoto et al., 2024), alignment with a principal query direction (Godey et al., 2025), deviation from neighboring keys (Liang et al., 2025), or value norm (Guo et al., 2024). Merging methods soften the same decision by folding evicted entries into retained ones. KVMerger (Wang et al., 2024) merges similar entries into attention-weighted pivots, and Zhang et al. (2024); Wan et al. (2024); Nawrot et al. (2024) use related rules. In all of these, the score of an entry is fixed before any other entry is removed.

Output-aware eviction. More recent methods score entries directly through the attention-output error induced by their removal (Goel et al., 2026; An et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026). CAOTE (Goel et al., 2026) and ReST-KV (An et al., 2026) derive the exact effect of deleting one entry for one query. OBCache (Gu et al., 2026) derives a second-order approximation in the style of Optimal Brain Damage (LeCun et al., 1989). CriticalKV (Feng et al., 2026) considers deletion of an arbitrary set for one query and derives an additive upper bound on the resulting output error for selection. These methods differ in how they estimate deletion error, but share a common restriction: candidates are evaluated with the retained cache held fixed.

Our work starts from the same output-reconstruction objective as CAOTE, ReST-KV, and OBCache but changes how it is used for selection. Instead of scoring one deletion against a fixed cache, we derive a quadratic surrogate of the output error over arbitrary deletions and reweightings of the retained entries, aggregated over many calibration queries, and let the retained entries compensate during greedy deletion of cache entries.

3 KV-Surgeon

In this section, we present our method for offline KV-cache compaction, KV-Surgeon. It compacts each attention head independently by selecting which original cache entries to delete, accounting for how the remaining entries can compensate for deleted ones, and then refits the retained entries to preserve the behavior of the original cache.

3.1 Problem formulation

We consider one layer and one attention head with TT cache entries. Cache entry jj consists of a key kj∈ℝdkk_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} and a value vj∈ℝdvv_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}. We describe the behavior of the head on NN calibration queries q1,…,qN∈ℝdkq_{1},\ldots,q_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} recorded from the model itself as described in Section 4.1. For query ii and cache entry jj, the corresponding logit is Zi​j≜qi⊤​kj/dkZ_{ij}\triangleq q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d_{k}}. The attention weight and output are

Pi​j≜eZi​j∑ℓ=1TeZi​ℓ,oi≜∑j=1TPi​j​vj.P_{ij}\triangleq\frac{e^{Z_{ij}}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}e^{Z_{i\ell}}},\qquad o_{i}\triangleq\sum_{j=1}^{T}P_{ij}v_{j}. (1)

Let V∈ℝT×dvV\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{v}} collect the values as rows and P∈ℝN×TP\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times T} the attention weights. The corresponding output matrix is then O=P​V∈ℝN×dvO=PV\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{v}}.

Compacted cache.

Given a budget t<Tt<T, which is allocated per head, we retain tt cache entries corresponding to some index set S⊆{1,…,T}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\} with |S|=t|S|=t, which we call the support. Each retained entry j∈Sj\in S keeps its original key kjk_{j} and is assigned an adapted value v^j∈ℝdv\widehat{v}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} and a positive attention multiplier wj>0w_{j}>0, which rescales the contribution of its entry before the softmax normalization. Together, the remaining keys kjk_{j}, adapted values v^j\widehat{v}_{j}, and attention multipliers wjw_{j} form the compacted cache. For query ii and entry jj, the attention weights and output of the compacted cache are given by

P^i​j≜wj​eZi​j∑ℓ∈Swℓ​eZi​ℓ=wj​Pi​j∑ℓ∈Swℓ​Pi​ℓ=wj​Pi​jμi,o^i≜∑j∈SP^i​j​v^j=1μi​∑j∈SPi​j​wj​v^j.\widehat{P}_{ij}\triangleq\frac{w_{j}e^{Z_{ij}}}{\sum_{\ell\in S}w_{\ell}e^{Z_{i\ell}}}=\frac{w_{j}P_{ij}}{\sum_{\ell\in S}w_{\ell}P_{i\ell}}=\frac{w_{j}P_{ij}}{\mu_{i}},\qquad\widehat{o}_{i}\triangleq\sum_{j\in S}\widehat{P}_{ij}\widehat{v}_{j}=\frac{1}{\mu_{i}}\sum_{j\in S}P_{ij}w_{j}\widehat{v}_{j}. (2)

Here,

μi≜∑j∈SPi​j​wj=∑j∈Swj​eZi​j∑ℓ=1TeZi​ℓ\mu_{i}\triangleq\sum_{j\in S}P_{ij}w_{j}=\frac{\sum_{j\in S}w_{j}e^{Z_{ij}}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}e^{Z_{i\ell}}} (3)

is the ratio between the compacted and original attention normalization terms. Let PS∈ℝN×|S|P_{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times|S|} contain the columns of PP indexed by SS, let w∈ℝ|S|w\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|} collect the multipliers, and let V^∈ℝ|S|×dv\widehat{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|\times d_{v}} collect the new values as rows. The vector of the normalization ratios is then μ≜(μ1,…,μN)⊤=PS​w\mu\triangleq(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{N})^{\top}=P_{S}w and the output of the compacted cache is O^=diag⁡(PS​w)−1​PS​diag⁡(w)​V^\widehat{O}=\operatorname{diag}(P_{S}w)^{-1}P_{S}\operatorname{diag}(w)\widehat{V}.

Compaction objective.

Our goal is for the compacted cache to preserve two properties of the original cache. First, its attention outputs O^\widehat{O} should be close to the outputs OO of the original, uncompacted cache. We measure the output error by

ℒ⁡(S,w,V^)≜∥O^−O∥F2.\mathcal{L}(S,w,\widehat{V})\triangleq\lVert\widehat{O}-O\rVert_{F}^{2}. (4)

Second, when combined with other context, such as a question, a system prompt, or other compacted chunks, its entries should collectively receive approximately the same share of attention as the original cache entries, i.e., ∑j∈Swj​eZi​j≈∑j=1TeZi​j\sum_{j\in S}w_{j}e^{Z_{ij}}\approx\sum_{j=1}^{T}e^{Z_{ij}}. Output preservation alone does not ensure this: scaling all wjw_{j} by the same constant leaves O^\widehat{O} unchanged but changes this sum. For a more detailed discussion, see Appendix H.

On the calibration queries, we express these two goals as follows, using the ratio μ\mu of the compacted and original normalization terms defined in 3

O^≈O,μ=PS​w≈𝟏.\widehat{O}\approx O,\qquad\mu=P_{S}w\approx\mathbf{1}. (5)

3.2 Tractable surrogate

Choosing the optimal support SS is difficult even if we consider only output preservation. For a fixed support SS, the output error ℒ⁡(S,w,V^)\mathcal{L}(S,w,\widehat{V}) depends on how well the multipliers ww and values V^\widehat{V} can be adjusted, so evaluating all (Tt)\binom{T}{t} possible supports is infeasible. In order to approximate this objective, we start from a larger support and sequentially delete entries. However, even assessing the cost of deleting one entry j∈Sj\in S requires re-optimizing ww and V^\widehat{V} on S∖{j}S\setminus\{j\}. Doing that for every candidate deletion at every step is still prohibitively expensive.

We therefore seek a surrogate objective that makes it inexpensive to compare candidate deletions while accounting for how the remaining entries can compensate. After removing an entry, we also want to reuse previous computations to evaluate the next deletions efficiently. Starting from 5, we derive a quadratic surrogate with these properties.

Attention as a ratio of two linear terms.

We introduce the variable U≜diag⁡(w)​V^∈ℝ|S|×dvU\triangleq\operatorname{diag}(w)\widehat{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|\times d_{v}}, whose row corresponding to entry j∈Sj\in S is uj⊤=wj​v^j⊤u_{j}^{\top}=w_{j}\widehat{v}_{j}^{\top} and which absorbs the attention multipliers ww into the values V^\widehat{V}. This is an exact change of variables: since wj>0w_{j}>0, we can recover the original values as v^j=uj/wj\widehat{v}_{j}=u_{j}/w_{j}. Substituting into 2, the output of the compacted cache can be written as the ratio

o^i=niμi,ni≜∑j∈SPi​j​uj∈ℝdv,μi=∑j∈SPi​j​wj∈ℝ.\widehat{o}_{i}=\frac{n_{i}}{\mu_{i}},\qquad n_{i}\triangleq\sum_{j\in S}P_{ij}u_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}},\qquad\mu_{i}=\sum_{j\in S}P_{ij}w_{j}\in\mathbb{R}. (6)

The numerator nin_{i} and the denominator μi\mu_{i} are linear in UU and ww, respectively.

For the original cache, the numerator is ∑j=1TPi​j​vj=oi\sum_{j=1}^{T}P_{ij}v_{j}=o_{i} and the denominator is ∑j=1TPi​j=1\sum_{j=1}^{T}P_{ij}=1, since every row of PP sums to one. Instead of searching for an o^i\widehat{o}_{i} matching this ratio, we ask the compacted cache to reproduce numerator and denominator separately, ni≈oin_{i}\approx o_{i} and μi≈1\mu_{i}\approx 1. The second condition is the mass requirement of 5, and together they imply o^i≈oi\widehat{o}_{i}\approx o_{i}. Define the residuals ri≜ni−oir_{i}\triangleq n_{i}-o_{i} and εi≜μi−1\varepsilon_{i}\triangleq\mu_{i}-1,

o^i−oi=ni−μi​oiμi=ri−εi​oiμi,hence∥o^i−oi∥2≤∥ri∥2+|εi|​∥oi∥2μi.\widehat{o}_{i}-o_{i}=\frac{n_{i}-\mu_{i}o_{i}}{\mu_{i}}=\frac{r_{i}-\varepsilon_{i}\,o_{i}}{\mu_{i}},\qquad\text{hence}\qquad\lVert\widehat{o}_{i}-o_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\lVert r_{i}\rVert_{2}+\lvert\varepsilon_{i}\rvert\,\lVert o_{i}\rVert_{2}}{\mu_{i}}. (7)

The output error is thus small whenever both residuals are small: a small εi\varepsilon_{i} also keeps μi\mu_{i} close to one.

Quadratic surrogate.

We construct a surrogate of 4 by summing the squared residuals from 7 over all queries. In matrix form, the rir_{i} are the rows of PS​U−O∈ℝN×dvP_{S}U-O\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{v}}, and the εi\varepsilon_{i} are the entries of μ−𝟏=PS​w−𝟏∈ℝN\mu-\mathbf{1}=P_{S}w-\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. A weight γ2>0\gamma^{2}>0 controls the relative importance of mass preservation (see Section A.3), giving

∥O−PS​U∥F2+γ2​∥𝟏−PS​w∥22=‖[Oγ​𝟏]−PS​[Uγ​w]‖F2.\lVert O-P_{S}U\rVert_{F}^{2}+\gamma^{2}\lVert\mathbf{1}-P_{S}w\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\begin{bmatrix}O&\gamma\mathbf{1}\end{bmatrix}-P_{S}\begin{bmatrix}U&\gamma w\end{bmatrix}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (8)

The original loss 4 couples ww and V^\widehat{V} through their products and the division by μi\mu_{i}, whereas for a fixed support SS, the quadratic surrogate separates the optimization of UU and ww into two linear least-squares problems with the same design matrix PS∈ℝN×|S|P_{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times|S|}. The right-hand side stacks the targets into [Oγ​𝟏]∈ℝN×(dv+1)[\,O\ \ \gamma\mathbf{1}\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times(d_{v}+1)} and the coefficients into [Uγ​w]∈ℝ|S|×(dv+1)[\,U\ \ \gamma w\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|\times(d_{v}+1)}, yielding a single linear least-squares problem with dv+1d_{v}+1 target columns.

Support-selection score.

In 8, UU is unconstrained, since any UU is attained by V^=diag⁡(w)−1​U\widehat{V}=\operatorname{diag}(w)^{-1}U, but the last column of [Uγ​w][\,U\ \ \gamma w\,] is constrained by w>0w>0. To obtain an unconstrained quadratic problem, we remove this constraint and replace [Uγ​w][\,U\ \ \gamma w\,] with a free matrix B∈ℝ|S|×(dv+1)B\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|\times(d_{v}+1)}. Each row of BB corresponds to a retained cache entry jj: its first dvd_{v} coefficients replace the weighted value wj​v^jw_{j}\widehat{v}_{j}, and its last coefficient replaces the scaled attention multiplier γ​wj\gamma w_{j}. These coefficients need not correspond to a valid compacted cache because the last coefficient can be negative. In practice, fewer than half a percent of the retained entries end with a negative coefficient in the last column (Appendix I), and valid multipliers are restored by the final refit (Section 3.4).

Finally, we add a small ridge penalty so that the regression has a unique solution for every support. With Y≜[Oγ​𝟏]∈ℝN×(dv+1)Y\triangleq[\,O\ \ \gamma\mathbf{1}\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times(d_{v}+1)}, we define the support score

ℱ⁡(S)≜minB⁡∥Y−PS​B∥F2+λ​∥B∥F2,λ>0.\mathcal{F}(S)\triangleq\min_{B}\lVert Y-P_{S}B\rVert_{F}^{2}+\lambda\lVert B\rVert_{F}^{2},\qquad\lambda>0. (9)

YY and λ\lambda stay fixed during support selection: YY depends only on the original cache, and λ\lambda is set once per head (Appendix B). For a fixed support SS, ℱ⁡(S)\mathcal{F}(S) is the minimum value of this quadratic objective after optimizing all coefficients in BB. Changing SS changes the available columns of PSP_{S} and therefore also the optimal coefficients: removing an entry requires the remaining coefficients to compensate for its absence.

3.3 Greedy elimination with closed-form compensation

With the support score ℱ⁡(S)\mathcal{F}(S) in place, we now develop a greedy elimination algorithm that uses it to choose which cache entries to retain. Starting from a support larger than the target budget tt, we repeatedly remove the entry whose deletion causes the smallest increase in ℱ⁡(S)\mathcal{F}(S), allowing the remaining coefficients to compensate at each step. The quadratic structure of 9 lets us compute both these loss increases and the compensating updates in closed form, using an approach developed in the pruning literature (Hassibi & Stork, 1993; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023). We first describe the optimal coefficients on the current support, then show how to evaluate and apply a deletion.

Optimal coefficients on the current support.

Each column of BB contains the coefficients used to reconstruct one target column of YY: either an output coordinate or the attention mass. In 9, these linear least-squares problems all have the same Hessian 2​(PS⊤​PS+λ​I)2(P_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I) (see Section A.2). A single |S|×|S||S|\times|S| inverse GG therefore suffices for all columns. Writing BB and GG for the optimal coefficients and shared inverse on the current support SS, we have

B=G​PS⊤​Y∈ℝ|S|×(dv+1),G≜(PS⊤​PS+λ​I)−1∈ℝ|S|×|S|.B=G\,P_{S}^{\top}Y\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|\times(d_{v}+1)},\qquad G\triangleq\big(P_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I\big)^{-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|\times|S|}. (10)

The current BB and GG suffice to evaluate every candidate deletion and obtain the optimal coefficients afterward, without solving another regression problem. For an entry j∈Sj\in S, we define its saliency sjs_{j} as the increase in the optimal surrogate objective when that entry is removed:

sj≜ℱ(S∖{j})−ℱ(S)=∥Bj,:∥22Gj​j.s_{j}\triangleq\mathcal{F}(S\setminus\{j\})-\mathcal{F}(S)=\frac{\lVert B_{j,:}\rVert_{2}^{2}}{G_{jj}}. (11)

The saliency sjs_{j} measures the surrogate loss increase after the remaining coefficients have been re-optimized. An entry can make a large contribution to the original outputs yet have low saliency if other retained entries can compensate for its removal.

Once an entry jj is selected for removal, we obtain the optimal coefficients and inverse for the reduced support directly from the current matrices. Writing −j-j for the indices in S∖{j}S\setminus\{j\}, the updates are

B←B−j,:−G−j,jBj,:Gj​j,G←G−j,−j−G−j,j​Gj,−jGj​j.B\leftarrow B_{-j,:}-\frac{G_{-j,j}B_{j,:}}{G_{jj}},\qquad G\leftarrow G_{-j,-j}-\frac{G_{-j,j}G_{j,-j}}{G_{jj}}. (12)

The updated BB is the exact minimizer of 9 on S∖{j}S\setminus\{j\}, and GG is the corresponding inverse Gram matrix. We repeatedly remove the entry with the smallest current saliency, update BB and GG, and recompute the remaining saliencies until |S|=t|S|=t, without solving another regression problem from scratch. A detailed derivation is given in Section A.4.

3.4 Implementation details

KV-Surgeon builds on the greedy elimination process described above, with a few practical additions. To reduce computational cost, we restrict the initial set of candidates, delete entries in blocks, and use a cheaper selection rule for heads that retain a relatively large fraction of their original cache entries. After selecting the support, we refit the attention multipliers ww and values V^\widehat{V} to obtain a valid compacted cache. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete method. We describe these additions below, with further implementation details in Appendix B and ablations in Section E.3.

Candidate pool. To limit the size of GG and the number of deletion steps, we first rank entries by a leave-one-out (LOO) score. We obtain it by removing entry jj in 2, keeping unit multipliers and the remaining values unchanged, and evaluating the output-preservation loss 4:

sjLOO≜∑i=1NPi​j2(1−Pi​j)2​∥vj−oi∥22.s_{j}^{\mathrm{LOO}}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{P_{ij}^{2}}{(1-P_{ij})^{2}}\lVert v_{j}-o_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}. (13)

LOO measures the exact output error on the original cache without adjusting the remaining entries, whereas the saliency in 11 measures the surrogate loss increase accounting for compensation. We keep the m=min⁡{T,⌈c​t⌉}m=\min\{T,\lceil ct\rceil\} entries with the largest sjLOOs_{j}^{\mathrm{LOO}} and perform greedy elimination only on this pool, using c=4c=4. We also use 13 directly as the score of the LOO baseline (Section 4.1). The score derivation and pool-size ablation are given in Section A.5 and Section E.3, respectively.

Block deletion. We select a block J⊂SJ\subset S containing the entries with the smallest current saliencies. Analogously to 12, the optimal coefficients and inverse for the reduced support R=S∖JR=S\setminus J are obtained by

B←BR,:−GR,JGJ,J−1BJ,:,G←GR,R−GR,JGJ,J−1GJ,R,R≜S∖J.B\leftarrow B_{R,:}-G_{R,J}G_{J,J}^{-1}B_{J,:},\qquad G\leftarrow G_{R,R}-G_{R,J}G_{J,J}^{-1}G_{J,R},\qquad R\triangleq S\setminus J. (14)

For any selected block JJ, these updates give the exact minimizer of the surrogate on S∖JS\setminus J. Selecting JJ by individual saliencies, however, need not minimize the joint deletion cost. Empirically, deleting multiple entries at once improves efficiency without hurting performance. Further implementation details are given in Appendix B.

Final refit. The support-selection procedure determines which entries to retain, but the unconstrained coefficients BB need not represent a valid compacted cache. We therefore discard BB and GG and refit the multipliers ww and values V^\widehat{V} on the selected support SS. Following Zweiger et al. (2026), we first minimize ∥𝟏−PS​w∥22\lVert\mathbf{1}-P_{S}w\rVert_{2}^{2} subject to box constraints on ww, obtaining positive multipliers that preserve the original attention mass as closely as possible. We then fix ww and optimize V^\widehat{V} to minimize the output-preservation loss 4. The resulting cache retains the original keys with refitted multipliers and values. See Appendix B for further details.

Mild-compaction fallback. For heads that retain a relatively large fraction of their original cache entries, we skip greedy elimination and the final refit, retaining the tt entries with the largest LOO scores, their original values, and unit multipliers. Since these heads undergo little compaction, this simpler procedure reduces computation with negligible accuracy loss. Further implementation details are given in Appendix B and the corresponding ablation in Section E.3.

4 Experiments

We compare KV-Surgeon to existing methods and show that it improves the cost–accuracy frontier across different models, benchmarks, and compaction ratios. We then analyze which part of the algorithm is the source of this improvement through controlled ablations. Finally, we study how much of the gain is retained when self-study calibration is replaced by a single repeat pass. Our code is available at github.com/ZIB-IOL/KV-Surgeon.

4.1 Experimental setup

Benchmarks and models. We evaluate offline KV-cache compaction on long-context multiple-choice question-answering tasks from QuALITY (Pang et al., 2022) and LongHealth (Adams et al., 2024), and code completion tasks from Long Code Arena (Bogomolov et al., 2024), where each compacted context is reused across many questions. We evaluate five models, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-12B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B (Yang et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Team et al., 2025), spanning three model families, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and different attention variants. Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 replaces Qwen3-4B on LongHealth and Long Code Arena because it supports longer contexts. We consider {100×,50×,20×,10×,5×}\{100\times,50\times,20\times,10\times,5\times\} compaction, with 50×50\times as the primary operating point. Dataset construction and evaluation details are given in Appendix C.

Protocol. All accuracies are means over five random seeds, with one standard error reported in the tables. All methods shown in the main comparison, except LLM summarization, use heterogeneous allocation of the global cache budget across heads. The allocation is computed once per model on data disjoint from the evaluation benchmarks following Zweiger et al. (2026) and kept fixed between methods. All methods using calibration additionally share the attention-multiplier parameterization and final cache refit of Section 3, so their comparisons isolate differences in support selection. KV-Surgeon hyperparameters are fixed once on Qwen3-4B with QuALITY at 50×50\times compaction and reused for all other models, benchmarks, and compaction ratios, i.e., KV-Surgeon does not require per-model or per-benchmark tuning.

Calibration and cost. To collect calibration queries, we use two different approaches. Cheap calibration queries are obtained by a repeat pass, which concatenates the context with a “repeat verbatim” prompt and another copy of the context (Kim et al., 2026). For self-study, the more expensive approach, we prompt the model to discuss the context multiple times and record the queries produced during answer generation (Eyuboglu et al., 2026). The suffix -fast denotes repeat-pass calibration for KV-Surgeon and AM-HAK. AM-OMP-CS is the cheap-solver setting of Zweiger et al. (2026), named AM-OMP-fast in the original work, and uses self-study queries. Pipeline time covers calibration-query generation and compaction, but excludes the context prefill shared by all methods and preprocessing performed once per model. Further timing and calibration details are given in Appendix C.

Baselines. Our main prior baseline is attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), for which we evaluate both AM-HighestAttentionKeys (AM-HAK) and AM-OMP using the authors’ implementation and hyperparameters. We also adapt several serving-time eviction methods to the offline setting (Appendix G) and include our adaptation of OBCache in the main experiments. LOO ranks entries by the exact single-deletion score of 13 and shares KV-Surgeon’s calibration queries, head-budget allocation, and final refit, providing a controlled comparison to independent selection. We additionally include LLM summarization and query-free baselines (Appendix D).

4.2 KV-Surgeon improves the cost–accuracy frontier

At 50×50\times compaction, both KV-Surgeon and KV-Surgeon-fast exceed the prior state of the art (Table 1). KV-Surgeon-fast reaches 63.9%63.9\% mean accuracy in 5454 seconds per context, compared with 63.2%63.2\% for AM-OMP in 763763 seconds, a 14.1×14.1\times reduction in pipeline time. Self-study calibration improves KV-Surgeon further to 65.1%65.1\% in 145145 seconds, 1.91.9 percentage points above AM-OMP at 5.3×5.3\times lower time. At comparable cost, KV-Surgeon-fast is 3.33.3 percentage points ahead of adapted OBCache, while KV-Surgeon is 3.03.0 points ahead of AM-HAK.

These gains are consistent across models and benchmarks. For both calibration methods, KV-Surgeon is best or tied for best within uncertainty on all eight model–benchmark pairs, while KV-Surgeon-fast is ahead of every other repeat-pass method beyond uncertainty. Thus, the more expensive AM-OMP variants no longer lie on the cost–accuracy frontier at our primary operating point (Figure 1).

The advantage of KV-Surgeon also persists across compaction ratios. Figure 2 shows mean accuracy over the eight model–benchmark pairs relative to KV-Surgeon. All prior methods are worse by more than two standard errors at every compaction ratio. The gap is largest between 100×100\times and 20×20\times compaction and narrows at 10×10\times and 5×5\times, where all methods approach the performance of the full-context ceiling. We therefore focus the analysis below on large compaction ratios, where support selection has the largest effect.

The same compute-time advantage transfers to project-level code completion on Long Code Arena (Table 12, Section D.1). At 50×50\times, KV-Surgeon and KV-Surgeon-fast match AM-OMP within uncertainty while using 9.79.7 and 21.521.5 times less compute time, respectively. At 20×20\times, KV-Surgeon has the highest point estimate, with AM-OMP-CS the only prior method within uncertainty at 6.76.7 times higher cost.

4.3 Sources of the performance gain

The gain over independent selection comes from compensating the surviving cache entries as the support changes. To isolate this effect, we keep the surrogate, candidate pool, calibration queries, and final refit fixed and disable only the compensating update: we delete entries based on the saliency 11 but do not apply the update 12 to the remaining entries, so the saliencies stay fixed and the elimination reduces to a single ranking of the candidate pool. At 50×50\times compaction on Qwen3-4B with QuALITY, this reduces accuracy from 66.9%66.9\% to 63.9%63.9\% (Table 2). KV-Surgeon without compensation also performs similarly to LOO, which uses the different deletion rule 13 and does not adapt the remaining entries at all. Replacing the saliency score alone does not explain the improvement. Rather, the gain comes from updating the remaining entries during selection. Additional controls that remove the opportunity for iterative compensation lead to the same conclusion (Appendices E and F).

The improvement is also not an artifact of the optimized allocation of the global cache budget across heads inherited from Zweiger et al. (2026). Under uniform allocation, KV-Surgeon remains 3.03.0 accuracy points ahead of AM-HAK (Appendix E). Compensation-aware support selection therefore provides an improvement that is orthogonal to that of the offline-compaction pipeline proposed by Zweiger et al. (2026).

4.4 Cheap calibration preserves most of the gain

KV-Surgeon is comparatively insensitive to how calibration queries are collected. Replacing self-study with a single repeat pass reduces pipeline time from 145145 to 5454 seconds per context at 50×50\times compaction while reducing mean accuracy by only 1.21.2 points. The same change is substantially more costly for AM-HAK, which loses 4.94.9 points (Table 1). This makes KV-Surgeon-fast not only cheaper, but sufficient to outperform all prior methods at the primary operating point.

This robustness persists across compaction ratios. Replacing self-study with repeat-pass calibration costs KV-Surgeon at most 1.21.2 points of mean accuracy at any compaction ratio, with the gap shrinking as more cache entries are retained. Detailed results across ratios are reported in Appendix D; Appendix F offers a hypothesis for this robustness.

5 Conclusion

Prior offline KV-cache compaction methods first deleted cache entries and then adapted the remaining ones. We showed that deletion and adaptation can be coupled efficiently, and that doing so improves accuracy. We derived a quadratic surrogate of the attention-output error that allows for an efficient greedy algorithm with compensation-aware selection: every candidate deletion is scored after the retained entries have compensated for it. The resulting method, KV-Surgeon, improves the cost–accuracy frontier at every compaction ratio on QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena with models from 4B to 30B parameters, and its fast variant exceeds all prior methods at two fifths of the cost of the strongest baseline. A controlled comparison attributes the gain over independent selection to compensation during selection, not to the surrogate.

Appendix A Derivations

A.1 The surrogate as a second-order Taylor expansion

An alternative route to the same surrogate starts with the exact output loss after substituting U=diag⁡(w)​V^U=\operatorname{diag}(w)\widehat{V}:

ℒ⁡(S,w,V^)=∑i=1N1μi2​‖(∑j∈SPi​j​uj−oi)+(1−μi)​oi‖22.\mathcal{L}(S,w,\widehat{V})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\mu_{i}^{2}}\left\lVert\left(\sum_{j\in S}P_{ij}u_{j}-o_{i}\right)+(1-\mu_{i})o_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}. (15)

Replacing μi−2\mu_{i}^{-2} by its value of one at the original cache gives the quadratic

𝒬⁡(S,w,U)≜∑i=1N‖∑j∈SPi​j​uj−μi​oi‖22.\mathcal{Q}(S,w,U)\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\lVert\sum_{j\in S}P_{ij}u_{j}-\mu_{i}o_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}. (16)

Dropping the cross term between the output and mass residuals separates the two terms:

∥O−PS​U∥F2+∑i=1N(∥oi∥2​(1−(PS​w)i))2.\lVert O-P_{S}U\rVert_{F}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl(\lVert o_{i}\rVert_{2}(1-(P_{S}w)_{i})\bigr)^{2}. (17)

Replacing the query-dependent weights ∥oi∥2\lVert o_{i}\rVert_{2} by the shared γ\gamma then gives 8. The quadratic 𝒬\mathcal{Q} in 16 is the second-order Taylor expansion of ℒ\mathcal{L} around the original cache. This supplies an alternative derivation of the surrogate in Section 3.2. The method represents a deletion by removing an index from SS, and a support SS and the original cache have parameters of different sizes. To place them in a common coordinate system we use, in this proof only, a full-length multiplier vector m∈ℝTm\in\mathbb{R}^{T} with mj=wjm_{j}=w_{j} for j∈Sj\in S and mj=0m_{j}=0 otherwise, and U~∈ℝT×dv\widetilde{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{v}} with rows mj​v^jm_{j}\widehat{v}_{j}, which vanish outside SS. Then ∑j∈SPi​j​uj⊤=Pi​U~\sum_{j\in S}P_{ij}u_{j}^{\top}=P_{i}\widetilde{U} and μi=Pi​m\mu_{i}=P_{i}m, where PiP_{i} is row ii of PP, so that

are functions of (U~,m)∈ℝT×dv×ℝT(\widetilde{U},m)\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{v}}\times\mathbb{R}^{T} whose domain contains the original cache (U~,m)=(V,𝟏)(\widetilde{U},m)=(V,\mathbf{1}). There the vector inside the norms is Pi​V−(Pi​𝟏)​oi=oi−oi=0P_{i}V-(P_{i}\mathbf{1})\,o_{i}=o_{i}-o_{i}=0 for every query, because Pi​V=oiP_{i}V=o_{i} by the definition of OO and Pi​𝟏=1P_{i}\mathbf{1}=1 since every row of PP is a softmax; hence ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} vanish together with their gradients. Write (U~,m)=(V+ΔU,𝟏+Δm)(\widetilde{U},m)=(V+\Delta_{U},\mathbf{1}+\Delta_{m}). Substituting, the vector inside the norms becomes Pi​(V+ΔU)−(Pi​(𝟏+Δm))​oi=(Pi​V−oi)+Pi​ΔU−(Pi​Δm)​oi=Pi​ΔU−(Pi​Δm)​oiP_{i}(V+\Delta_{U})-\bigl(P_{i}(\mathbf{1}+\Delta_{m})\bigr)\,o_{i}=(P_{i}V-o_{i})+P_{i}\Delta_{U}-(P_{i}\Delta_{m})\,o_{i}=P_{i}\Delta_{U}-(P_{i}\Delta_{m})\,o_{i}, again by Pi​V=oiP_{i}V=o_{i} and Pi​𝟏=1P_{i}\mathbf{1}=1. A.2 Hessian structure of the surrogate

We compare the quadratic objectives of Section 3.2 through their Hessians in the unknowns (U,w)(U,w). Stack the unknowns as x≜(U:,1,…,U:,dv,w)∈ℝ|S|​(dv+1)x\triangleq(U_{:,1},\ldots,U_{:,d_{v}},w)\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|(d_{v}+1)}, where U:,cU_{:,c} is column cc of UU, and write O:,cO_{:,c} for column cc of OO.

After freezing the normalization. The frozen objective 16 is ∥PS​U−diag⁡(PS​w)​O∥F2\lVert P_{S}U-\operatorname{diag}(P_{S}w)O\rVert_{F}^{2}. Column cc of diag⁡(PS​w)​O\operatorname{diag}(P_{S}w)O is diag(O:,c)PSw\operatorname{diag}(O_{:,c})P_{S}w, so

∑i=1N∥(∑j∈SPi​juj−oi)+(1−μi)oi∥22=∑c=1dv∥PSU:,c−diag(O:,c)PSw∥22.\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big\lVert\Big(\sum_{j\in S}P_{ij}u_{j}-o_{i}\Big)+(1-\mu_{i})o_{i}\Big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{c=1}^{d_{v}}\big\lVert P_{S}U_{:,c}-\operatorname{diag}(O_{:,c})P_{S}w\big\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This is a quadratic in xx. Its Hessian has the diagonal blocks 2​PS⊤​PS2P_{S}^{\top}P_{S} for each column U:,cU_{:,c}, the diagonal block 2​PS⊤​diag⁡(∥o1∥22,…,∥oN∥22)​PS2P_{S}^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(\lVert o_{1}\rVert_{2}^{2},\ldots,\lVert o_{N}\rVert_{2}^{2})P_{S} for ww, and the off-diagonal blocks −2PS⊤diag(O:,c)PS-2P_{S}^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(O_{:,c})P_{S} between U:,cU_{:,c} and ww. The off-diagonal blocks are the Hessian of the cross term in 16: expanding the square gives 2​∑i⟨∑jPi​j​uj−oi,(1−μi)​oi⟩2\sum_{i}\langle\sum_{j}P_{ij}u_{j}-o_{i},\,(1-\mu_{i})o_{i}\rangle, whose bilinear part in (U,w)(U,w) is −2∑cU:,c⊤PS⊤diag(O:,c)PSw-2\sum_{c}U_{:,c}^{\top}P_{S}^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(O_{:,c})P_{S}w. Because of these blocks, the columns of UU and the multipliers are not separate regressions on PSP_{S}. Scoring a deletion, or computing the coefficients after one, requires the inverse of the full Hessian of dimension |S|​(dv+1)|S|(d_{v}+1) instead of an |S|×|S||S|\times|S| matrix, which multiplies the memory by (dv+1)2(d_{v}+1)^{2} and the cost of every update by at least the same factor.

After dropping the cross term. The objective 17 is a function of UU plus a function of ww, so its Hessian is block diagonal, with the blocks 2​PS⊤​PS2P_{S}^{\top}P_{S} for the columns of UU and the block 2​PS⊤​diag⁡(∥o1∥22,…,∥oN∥22)​PS2P_{S}^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(\lVert o_{1}\rVert_{2}^{2},\ldots,\lVert o_{N}\rVert_{2}^{2})P_{S} for ww. Every column can be optimized on its own. The multipliers, however, have a different Gram matrix from the values, so greedy elimination would carry two inverses and update both after every deletion.

After replacing the weights by γ\gamma. In 8 the mass term is γ2​∥𝟏−PS​w∥22=∥γ​𝟏−PS​(γ​w)∥22\gamma^{2}\lVert\mathbf{1}-P_{S}w\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lVert\gamma\mathbf{1}-P_{S}(\gamma w)\rVert_{2}^{2}, a regression of the column γ​𝟏\gamma\mathbf{1} on PSP_{S} in the unknown γ​w\gamma w, with Gram matrix PS⊤​PSP_{S}^{\top}P_{S}. All dv+1d_{v}+1 diagonal blocks of the Hessian are now 2​PS⊤​PS2P_{S}^{\top}P_{S} and there are no off-diagonal blocks. The ridge in 9 adds 2​λ​I2\lambda I to each block, so the Hessian of 9 in BB consists of dv+1d_{v}+1 identical blocks 2​(PS⊤​PS+λ​I)2(P_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I).

Closed form. Expanding 9 gives

∥Y−PS​B∥F2+λ​∥B∥F2=tr⁡(Y⊤​Y)−2​tr⁡(B⊤​PS⊤​Y)+tr⁡(B⊤​(PS⊤​PS+λ​I)​B).\lVert Y-P_{S}B\rVert_{F}^{2}+\lambda\lVert B\rVert_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(Y^{\top}Y)-2\operatorname{tr}(B^{\top}P_{S}^{\top}Y)+\operatorname{tr}\big(B^{\top}(P_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I)B\big).

The matrix PS⊤​PS+λ​IP_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I is positive definite for λ>0\lambda>0, since x⊤​(PS⊤​PS+λ​I)​x=∥PS​x∥22+λ​∥x∥22>0x^{\top}(P_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I)x=\lVert P_{S}x\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\lVert x\rVert_{2}^{2}>0 for x≠0x\neq 0. Inserting the minimizer and using (PS⊤​PS+λ​I)​B=PS⊤​Y(P_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I)B=P_{S}^{\top}Y for the first equality and G⁡(PS⊤​PS+λ​I)​G=GG(P_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I)G=G for the second,

ℱ⁡(S)=tr⁡(Y⊤​Y)−tr⁡(B⊤​(PS⊤​PS+λ​I)​B)=tr⁡(Y⊤​Y)−tr⁡(Y⊤​PS​G​PS⊤​Y).\mathcal{F}(S)=\operatorname{tr}(Y^{\top}Y)-\operatorname{tr}\big(B^{\top}(P_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I)B\big)=\operatorname{tr}(Y^{\top}Y)-\operatorname{tr}\big(Y^{\top}P_{S}GP_{S}^{\top}Y\big). (18)

A.3 Scale of the mass term

In 17 the mass error of query ii is weighted by ∥oi∥22\lVert o_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}: a query with a large output is hurt more by a given relative mass deficit. These weights depend neither on ww nor on SS, so the mass term of 17 could be minimized as it stands, with the Gram matrix PS⊤​diag⁡(∥o1∥22,…,∥oN∥22)​PSP_{S}^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(\lVert o_{1}\rVert_{2}^{2},\ldots,\lVert o_{N}\rVert_{2}^{2})P_{S}. Carrying it through the elimination would require a second inverse next to GG, updated after every deletion. Replacing ∥oi∥2\lVert o_{i}\rVert_{2} by one common scalar γ\gamma gives the mass term the Gram matrix PS⊤​PSP_{S}^{\top}P_{S} of the output term, so that one inverse serves all dv+1d_{v}+1 columns (Section A.2).

We set γ≜γ0​RMSi​∥oi∥2=γ0​(N−1​∑i∥oi∥22)1/2\gamma\triangleq\gamma_{0}\operatorname{RMS}_{i}\lVert o_{i}\rVert_{2}=\gamma_{0}\,(N^{-1}\sum_{i}\lVert o_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2})^{1/2} with a dimensionless γ0>0\gamma_{0}>0. The RMS keeps the mass column of YY on the scale of the output columns: for a uniform relative mass deficit 1−μi≡ϵ1-\mu_{i}\equiv\epsilon, the mass term of 17 is ϵ2​∑i∥oi∥22\epsilon^{2}\sum_{i}\lVert o_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2} and that of 8 is N​γ2​ϵ2N\gamma^{2}\epsilon^{2}, and the two agree for every ϵ\epsilon if and only if γ0=1\gamma_{0}=1. The factor γ0\gamma_{0} therefore sets the weight of the mass term relative to the output term, with γ0=1\gamma_{0}=1 matching the cost that a uniform deficit has under 17. We use γ0=1\gamma_{0}=1 throughout (Appendix C). Setting γ0=0\gamma_{0}=0 removes the mass term from the surrogate and changes accuracy within one standard error (Section E.3).

A.4 Deletion saliencies and compensation

We derive the saliency 11 and the updates 12 and 14 from the block structure of the inverse GG. Throughout, SS is the current support, A≜PS⊤​PS+λ​IA\triangleq P_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I, G=A−1G=A^{-1}, and B=G​PS⊤​YB=GP_{S}^{\top}Y as in 10. Rows and columns of AA, GG, and BB are indexed by the elements of SS, so that an entry keeps its index when other entries are deleted. For j∈Sj\in S, −j-j denotes the index set S∖{j}S\setminus\{j\}: G−j,−jG_{-j,-j} is GG without row and column jj, G−j,jG_{-j,j} is column jj of GG without its jj-th entry, and B−j,:B_{-j,:} is BB without row jj. We write pj∈ℝNp_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} for column jj of PP, the attention weights of all queries on entry jj.

Deleting an entry removes a row and a column of AA. Entry (k,l)(k,l) of PS⊤​PSP_{S}^{\top}P_{S} is pk⊤​plp_{k}^{\top}p_{l} and involves only the columns kk and ll. Removing column jj from PSP_{S} removes row and column jj from PS⊤​PSP_{S}^{\top}P_{S} and changes no other entry, and λ​I\lambda I loses the same row and column. This requires the same λ\lambda on both supports: a ridge that changes with SS would change the remaining entries as well.

the ridge-regularized residual of regressing the attention column of entry jj on the attention columns of the other retained entries. The saliency is therefore the squared coefficient magnitude of entry jj times the part of its attention column that the other retained columns do not reproduce, plus the ridge. An entry with a large coefficient is cheap to delete when its attention column lies close to the span of the other columns, and an entry with a small coefficient is expensive to delete when its attention column lies far from that span.
