A.5 The single-deletion score

The score of 13 is the one case in which the exact loss of 4 has a closed form: a single deletion with every other cache parameter at its original value, S={1,…,T}∖{j}S=\{1,\ldots,T\}\setminus\{j\}, w=𝟏w=\mathbf{1}, and v^k=vk\widehat{v}_{k}=v_{k} for k∈Sk\in S. Then U=VSU=V_{S}, μi=1−Pi​j\mu_{i}=1-P_{ij}, and ∑k∈SPi​k​vk−μi​oi=(oi−Pi​j​vj)−(1−Pi​j)​oi=−Pi​j​(vj−oi)\sum_{k\in S}P_{ik}v_{k}-\mu_{i}o_{i}=(o_{i}-P_{ij}v_{j})-(1-P_{ij})\,o_{i}=-P_{ij}(v_{j}-o_{i}), so 2 and 4 give

o^i−oi=−Pi​j1−Pi​j​(vj−oi),ℒ=∑i=1NPi​j2(1−Pi​j)2​∥vj−oi∥22=sjLOO.\widehat{o}_{i}-o_{i}=-\frac{P_{ij}}{1-P_{ij}}\,(v_{j}-o_{i}),\qquad\mathcal{L}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{P_{ij}^{2}}{(1-P_{ij})^{2}}\lVert v_{j}-o_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}=s_{j}^{\mathrm{LOO}}.

Goel et al. (2026) and An et al. (2026) derive the per-query error for serving-time eviction, with queries read from the prompt suffix; summing its squared norm over the calibration queries carries it to the offline setting. The error is the product of two factors. The renormalization factor Pi​j/(1−Pi​j)P_{ij}/(1-P_{ij}) is large for a heavy hitter (Zhang et al., 2023) with Pi​jP_{ij} near one, because the mass of the deleted entry is redistributed over retained entries that hold little mass themselves. The value novelty vj−oiv_{j}-o_{i} is small when the entry carries what the head already retrieves, so even a heavily attended entry can be deleted at no cost if its value is close to the current output. KV-Surgeon uses the score in three roles: as the prefilter that forms the candidate pool, as the selection rule of the mild-compaction fallback, and, followed by the same final refit, as the controlled baseline LOO of Section 4.3. Its second-order truncation, the diagonal Hj​jH_{jj} of Section A.1, drops the factor (1−Pi​j)−2(1-P_{ij})^{-2}.

Appendix B Algorithm and implementation

Algorithm 1 in Section 3.4 gives the complete procedure for one attention head. This section provides the hyperparameters, solvers, and computational details.

Multipliers as logit biases. For every retained entry j∈Sj\in S, the compacted cache stores the original key kjk_{j}, the refit value v^j\widehat{v}_{j}, and the logarithm log⁡wj\log w_{j} of its multiplier. At inference, log⁡wj\log w_{j} is added to the logit of entry jj before the softmax, so that the entry contributes eZi​j+log⁡wj=wj​eZi​je^{Z_{ij}+\log w_{j}}=w_{j}e^{Z_{ij}} to the unnormalized attention of query ii, which is 2. The bound e−β≤wj≤eβe^{-\beta}\leq w_{j}\leq e^{\beta} of the final refit is the bound |log⁡wj|≤β\lvert\log w_{j}\rvert\leq\beta on the logit bias of any single entry; it bounds the shift that compaction introduces and leaves the original logit Zi​jZ_{ij} unchanged. Mass preservation, μi≈1\mu_{i}\approx 1, keeps the total unnormalized attention of the compacted cache at that of the original cache, so that the compacted cache draws the same share of attention when it is served next to other tokens (Appendix H).

Candidate pool and ridge. The pool consists of the m=min⁡{T,⌈c​t⌉}m=\min\{T,\lceil ct\rceil\} entries with the largest scores 13, with c=4c=4. The score is evaluated with a floor, Pi​j2/((1−Pi​j)2+10−3)P_{ij}^{2}/((1-P_{ij})^{2}+10^{-3}), which bounds the weight of entries that receive almost all attention of a query; the LOO baseline uses the same evaluation. The minimum matters for heads with T/c<t≤τ​TT/c<t\leq\tau T, whose pool is the whole cache. The ridge is set relative to the scale of the Gram matrix on the pool, λ=λ0​tr⁡(PS⊤​PS)/m\lambda=\lambda_{0}\operatorname{tr}(P_{S}^{\top}P_{S})/m with λ0=0.01\lambda_{0}=0.01, computed once when the pool is formed and kept fixed for all later supports. A fixed λ\lambda is required for the updates 12 and 14 to be exact, because the Gram matrix of a reduced support is a principal submatrix of the current one only if both carry the same ridge (Section A.4). Since mm can exceed NN, PS⊤​PSP_{S}^{\top}P_{S} is singular on the pool in general, and the ridge is what makes GG well defined there. The inverse GG and the coefficients B=G​PS⊤​YB=GP_{S}^{\top}Y are computed explicitly once, on the pool, from a Cholesky factorization of PS⊤​PS+λ​IP_{S}^{\top}P_{S}+\lambda I; if the factorization fails, λ\lambda is increased tenfold, at most three times.

Block deletions. Each elimination step deletes the nb=32n_{b}=32 entries with the smallest saliencies; the last step deletes min⁡{nb,|S|−t}\min\{n_{b},|S|-t\} entries, so that the loop ends at |S|=t|S|=t exactly. The updates 14 require solving linear systems with the nb×nbn_{b}\times n_{b} matrix GJ,JG_{J,J}, which is positive definite as a principal submatrix of GG. Compared with single deletions, the block step computes the saliencies once per block rather than once per deletion and runs the updates as matrix products with nbn_{b} columns; the arithmetic count is the same.

Final refit. After the elimination, BB and GG are discarded, and the multipliers and values are solved on SS in two ordered steps, following the refit of attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026). The multipliers solve the box-constrained least-squares problem

w≜arg​mine−β≤wj≤eβ⁡∥𝟏−PS​w∥22,β=3.w\triangleq\argmin_{e^{-\beta}\leq w_{j}\leq e^{\beta}}\ \lVert\mathbf{1}-P_{S}w\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad\beta=3. (22)

The box restores the positivity dropped in Section 3.2 and bounds the logit bias of every entry. The solver is that of Zweiger et al. (2026) and solves 22 approximately. It works with the unnormalized attention E=exp⁡(Q​K⊤/dk−max)E=\exp(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}}-\max), the row maximum of the logits subtracted, and its row sums ss, so that P=diag⁡(s)−1​EP=\operatorname{diag}(s)^{-1}E, and minimizes ∥ES​w−s∥22\lVert E_{S}w-s\rVert_{2}^{2}, which is 22 with row ii scaled by sis_{i}. The unconstrained least-squares solution is computed by a QR solve, clamped to the box, and then refined by two projected gradient steps with step size 1/∥ES∥221/\lVert E_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}, clamping after each step; the spectral norm is estimated by three power iterations. With ww fixed, the normalized attention matrix of the compacted cache is P^≜diag⁡(PS​w)−1​PS​diag⁡(w)\widehat{P}\triangleq\operatorname{diag}(P_{S}w)^{-1}P_{S}\operatorname{diag}(w), cf. 2, and the values solve the linear least-squares problem

V^≜arg​minV^⁡∥P^​V^−O∥F2,\widehat{V}\triangleq\argmin_{\widehat{V}}\ \lVert\widehat{P}\widehat{V}-O\rVert_{F}^{2}, (23)

which is minV^⁡ℒ⁡(S,w,V^)\min_{\widehat{V}}\mathcal{L}(S,w,\widehat{V}), the exact output-preservation loss 4 for the chosen support and multipliers. All dvd_{v} columns of V^\widehat{V} share the Gram matrix P^⊤​P^\widehat{P}^{\top}\widehat{P} and are solved at once. They are computed by a least-squares solve; if the solve fails numerically, the normal equations (P^⊤​P^+10−6​a¯​I)​V^=P^⊤​O(\widehat{P}^{\top}\widehat{P}+10^{-6}\bar{a}I)\,\widehat{V}=\widehat{P}^{\top}O are solved by a Cholesky factorization instead, where a¯\bar{a} is the mean diagonal of P^⊤​P^\widehat{P}^{\top}\widehat{P}. The order of the two solves is forced: P^\widehat{P} depends on ww through diag⁡(w)\operatorname{diag}(w) and through PS​wP_{S}w, so the values have to be solved after the multipliers. The minimizer of 23 is unique if and only if PSP_{S} has full column rank, which cannot hold for t>Nt>N.

Mild-compaction fallback. Heads whose budget exceeds the fraction τ=0.3\tau=0.3 of their cache, t>τ​Tt>\tau T, skip the pool, the elimination, and the final refit: they retain the tt entries with the largest scores 13, their original values, and unit multipliers. Eviction is near-lossless at such mild compaction, the O⁡(t3)O(t^{3}) solves are largest for exactly these heads, and for t>Nt>N the value solve 23 is underdetermined. Disabling the fallback leaves accuracy unchanged and adds 37%37\% to pipeline time (Section E.3).

Complexity. Forming the Gram matrix of a pool of mm candidates costs O⁡(N​m2)O(Nm^{2}) and its inverse O⁡(m3)O(m^{3}); the right-hand side PS⊤​YP_{S}^{\top}Y costs O⁡(N​m​dv)O(Nmd_{v}) and the initial coefficients B=G​PS⊤​YB=GP_{S}^{\top}Y cost O⁡(m2​dv)O(m^{2}d_{v}). In each elimination step, the saliencies cost O​(|S|​(dv+1))O(|S|(d_{v}+1)) given BB and the diagonal of GG, the update of BB costs O⁡(|S|​nb​(dv+1)+nb3)O(|S|n_{b}(d_{v}+1)+n_{b}^{3}), and the update of GG costs O⁡(|S|2​nb)O(|S|^{2}n_{b}). Summed over the (m−t)/nb(m-t)/n_{b} steps, the loop costs O⁡(m3+m2​dv)O(m^{3}+m^{2}d_{v}), the same count as m−tm-t single deletions. The elimination on a pool of mm entries thus costs O⁡(N​m2+m3+N​m​dv+m2​dv)O(Nm^{2}+m^{3}+Nmd_{v}+m^{2}d_{v}) per head, and its memory is dominated by the m×mm\times m matrix GG. The pool bounds mm by c​tct, so these costs grow with the budget tt and not with the cache size TT; eliminating from the full cache instead changes accuracy within noise at 3.8×3.8\times the compaction time (Section E.3). The fallback removes the O⁡(t3)O(t^{3}) terms for the heads with the largest budgets.

Hyperparameters. All hyperparameters were fixed once on Qwen3-4B with QuALITY at 50×50\times and reused unchanged for every other model, benchmark, and ratio (Appendix C): the mass weight γ0=1\gamma_{0}=1 (Section A.3), the relative ridge λ0=0.01\lambda_{0}=0.01, the pool factor c=4c=4, the block size nb=32n_{b}=32, the fallback threshold τ=0.3\tau=0.3, and the multiplier bound β=3\beta=3. Section E.3 varies γ0\gamma_{0}, cc, and τ\tau.

Appendix C Experimental details

This section records what is needed to reproduce and read the experiments; Section 4.1 gives the summary. Section C.1 states the protocol and conventions and Section C.2 breaks down where the pipeline time goes.

C.1 Protocol and conventions

Task and benchmarks.

The model reads a context once, the resulting cache is compacted once by a target factor between 5×5\times and 100×100\times, and all benchmark questions about that context are answered from the compacted cache, so calibration and compaction are one-time costs per context. QuALITY uses the dev split, articles 0–49, with n=894n=894 multiple-choice questions; one article is one context. LongHealth consists of 20 fictional patient records, grouped into four contexts of five patients with roughly 60k tokens each; each record is compacted as its own chunk at the same ratio and the compacted chunks are concatenated (Appendix H), and all n=400n=400 multiple-choice questions are evaluated against their contexts. Accuracy is the percentage of correctly answered questions. Answers are extracted from the generated text, and questions whose answer cannot be parsed count as incorrect; parse rates are checked per run and are uniformly high in the reported cells, so parsing does not drive the reported differences. All eight model and benchmark combinations are reported.

Compaction ratio and per-head budgets.

The compaction factor, 5×5\times to 100×100\times, is the nominal ratio of the original cache size to the compacted one. Cache-side methods are reported at the nominal ratio because measured effective ratios agree with it to within one percent. Heads differ widely in how much compaction they tolerate, so the compaction factor is a global budget rather than a per-head prescription. Head (ℓ,h)(\ell,h) receives its own retained fraction rℓ​hr_{\ell h}, subject to the constraint that meanℓ​h⁡rℓ​h\operatorname{mean}_{\ell h}r_{\ell h} equals the reciprocal of the compaction factor; each head is additionally capped at rℓ​h≤0.75r_{\ell h}\leq 0.75, and the budget a capped head cannot use is redistributed to the other heads in proportion to their shares, so the global ratio is preserved. The allocation is computed once per model on contexts disjoint from the benchmark contexts, following the procedure introduced by Zweiger et al. (2026). We measure per head how the log-perplexity of model-generated reference answers degrades as that head alone is compressed, and we allocate the budget along these influence curves. The solver is ratio-agnostic: it finds one set of per-head proportions that works across all target ratios, and this single allocation is rescaled to each compaction factor. Every method in a table consumes the same allocation, so differences between rows are attributable to selection and refit alone; the published configuration of KVzip, reported only in Table 16, is the deliberate exception. Uniform per-head budgets serve as an ablation (Appendix E).

Calibration tiers.

All implemented methods score positions against calibration queries recorded from the model itself and, except AM-OMP, come in two tiers that differ mainly in how these queries are generated. The fast tier prompts the model to reproduce the context and records the query vectors of that single pass. The self-study tier additionally generates self-study conversations about the context, which cost more time but match the future workload better. AM-HAK-fast and KV-Surgeon-fast are the fast variants of AM-HAK and KV-Surgeon. AM-OMP, AM-OMP-CS, and KV-Surgeon are self-study methods; AM-OMP-CS is the cheap-solver setting of Zweiger et al. (2026), named AM-OMP-fast there, which selects several keys per greedy step and refits less often. After selecting which positions to keep, every calibrated method applies the same support-fixed refit of the retained multipliers and values (Section 3.4), so accuracy differences between them reflect the selection rule. AM-OMP is evaluated only at the most aggressive ratios because its runtime grows steeply with the retention budget.

Calibration queries.

Self-study generates five conversations per context with vLLM: a verbatim repetition of the context, a summary, an aggregation of key facts, a JSON structuring of the context, and three self-written questions with answers. The repetition is teacher-forced, with the context itself as the answer; the summary, aggregation, and JSON conversations are answered without thinking (at most 20482048 tokens, temperature 0.70.7, top-pp 0.80.8, top-kk 2020); the question conversation uses thinking for both writing and answering the questions (at most 81928192 and 40964096 tokens, temperature 0.60.6, top-pp 0.950.95, top-kk 2020). The calibration queries are the query vectors of the answer tokens, capped at 50,00050{,}000 per attention head by random subsampling. The repeat pass is the repetition conversation alone, that is, a single forward pass over the context, the repeat prompt, and a second copy of the context, without any generation. Queries are extracted on-policy, following Zweiger et al. (2026): layer 00 is compacted with the original queries, and for each later layer the same sequences are run through the model with the already compacted earlier layers in place, so every layer is compacted against the queries it receives at inference.

Replication and uncertainty.

Each cell is the mean over five replicate runs with explicit seeds, and the grey number is the standard error over these runs; a single run is noisy to about ±1.5\pm 1.5 points at n=894n=894 and ±2.0\pm 2.0 at n=400n=400, comparable to many method gaps, so we only trust orderings that survive the seed error bars. These standard errors measure generation noise under fixed contexts and questions, not uncertainty over the population of contexts, and LongHealth contributes only four composite contexts; generalization rests on the spread of the margins across the eight combinations in Appendix D. Full-context ceilings come from seed-replicated runs without compaction under the same protocol.

Timing conventions.

Pipeline time is the average wall-clock per context spent on calibration query generation plus compaction, in seconds. It excludes prefilling the context to extract its cache, answer generation, and answer extraction, all of which are common to all methods. Query-free methods therefore report compaction time alone. All runs are single-job SLURM runs on machines with H200 GPUs, launched with the same tooling, so times are comparable within a table; comparisons across models should be treated as indicative. Every table splits calibrated methods by calibration tier, repeat-pass above self-study; AM-OMP-CS uses self-study queries and sits in the self-study group.

Defaults.

The method defaults were fixed once on Qwen3-4B with QuALITY at 50×50\times and reused unchanged for every other model, benchmark, and ratio: the mass-term scale γ0=1\gamma_{0}=1, so that γ\gamma is the RMS norm of the full-cache outputs; the ridge λ0=0.01\lambda_{0}=0.01, applied relative to the mean diagonal of PS⊤​PSP_{S}^{\top}P_{S} on the candidate pool rather than as an absolute penalty; the block size nb=32n_{b}=32 deletions per elimination step; the candidate pool of m=min⁡{T,⌈4​t⌉}m=\min\{T,\lceil 4t\rceil\} entries; the threshold τ=0.3\tau=0.3 on the retained fraction t/Tt/T above which a head is left to plain eviction; and, in the final refit, the bound |log⁡wj|≤β=3|\log w_{j}|\leq\beta=3 on the served logit biases, that is, wj∈[e−3,e3]w_{j}\in[e^{-3},e^{3}], the interval that Table 18 refers to. Appendix E varies γ0\gamma_{0}, the pool, and the threshold; Appendix B describes how each hyperparameter enters the algorithm.

C.2 Where the time goes

Query generation sets the cost of the self-study tier.

Self-study query generation is a sampled generation pass over the context and costs the same whichever method consumes the queries: 2929 to 3333 seconds per QuALITY article and 193193 to 341341 per LongHealth context on the dense models, 3.43.4 to 5.85.8 ms per token, and 162162 and 10621062 seconds on Qwen3-30B-A3B, whose mixture-of-experts decoding runs four to five times slower per token under vLLM. A repeat pass, including re-extraction of its query vectors, costs 55 to 160160 seconds at 50×50\times on the dense models and on Qwen3-30B-A3B with QuALITY, and about 300300 seconds on Qwen3-30B-A3B with LongHealth; the query-free methods need no pass at all. Table 3 splits the self-study pipeline for LOO, KV-Surgeon, and AM-HAK, which consume the same queries. At 50×50\times, compaction is 33 to 25%25\% of the pipeline for all three, so the spread of their pipeline times in Appendix D, 22 to 12%12\%, comes entirely from the compaction step, while the order-of-magnitude gaps are between tiers.

Compaction grows with the retained fraction.

The compaction step of KV-Surgeon costs 1.4×1.4\times that of LOO at 50×50\times and 1.81.8 to 2.3×2.3\times at 5×5\times, because the block solve grows with the candidate pool: the log-log slope of compaction time against the retained fraction is 0.450.45 to 0.60.6 for LOO and AM-HAK and 0.650.65 to 0.950.95 for KV-Surgeon, and since query generation does not depend on the compaction factor, the compaction share rises from about 20%20\% to 5050–60%60\% across the grid on the dense models. Gemma-3-12B’s compaction is small because five of every six layers use sliding-window attention and only the global layers are compacted.

Appendix D Full results

The tables that follow cover one model and benchmark combination each and report QA accuracy and pipeline time for every method at all five compaction ratios, under the protocol of Appendix C. The conventions are the same throughout and are stated once here. Rows are grouped as in Table 1, query-free, repeat-pass, and self-study, separated by midrules, and the best accuracy per ratio within each group is bold; an entry is underlined when it trails the bold entry by at most two standard errors of the difference, computed from the two seed standard errors, so that bold without any underlined entry in the same group and column marks a separation beyond seed noise. Time is pipeline time per context in seconds; LongHealth contexts are about eight times longer than QuALITY articles, so every method costs roughly an order of magnitude more there. ‘–’ marks ratios a method does not reach: AM-OMP and AM-OMP-CS are capped because their solver cost grows with the retention budget. Summarization replaces the context by a model-generated summary of it. We use three prompts that lead to summaries of different lengths; the summary length is not a size parameter, so summarization has no table row, and Tables 1 and 1 report the prompt whose resulting cache size was closest to 50×50\times compaction.

Observations across the grids.

Three regularities are not visible in Table 1. First, mild compaction saturates: averaged over the eight combinations, the self-study methods span 54.754.7 to 59.359.3 points at 100×100\times but only 72.972.9 to 73.773.7 at 5×5\times against a ceiling of 74.074.0, and Llama-3.1-8B on QuALITY reaches its ceiling of 62.7%62.7\% at 20×20\times, so that combination is informative only at 50×50\times and 100×100\times. Second, KV-Surgeon is never behind beyond noise at the cell level: it is bold in 3232 of the 4040 self-study cells and within noise of the best in the other eight, and its largest deficit anywhere is 1.31.3 points, to an AM-OMP variant costing far more. Third, KV-Surgeon-fast is bold or within noise in 3737 of the 4040 repeat-pass cells and separated from every other repeat-pass method in all 1616 cells at 50×50\times and 100×100\times; its three losses beyond noise are all at 10×10\times and 5×5\times and at most 1.81.8 points.

Query-free baselines.

Q-Filters, StreamingLLM, and the L2L_{2} key-norm heuristic use the same optimized per-head budgets as every other method and need no calibration pass. Q-Filters is the best of them at every ratio, with a mean of 46.5%46.5\% at 50×50\times over the seven combinations that report all three, where KV-Surgeon-fast reaches 63.8%63.8\% on the same seven for about forty more seconds per context, so at this compaction, calibration is necessary.

D.1 Long Code Arena

Table 12 reports project-level code completion on Long Code Arena (Bogomolov et al., 2024) with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, the experiment behind the last paragraph of Section 4.2. The benchmark is the large_context configuration of its project-level code completion task: each datapoint is a repository snapshot at a fixed commit, one held-out completion file, and a list of target lines in that file.

Contexts and questions.

We walk the test split in order and keep the first snapshot of each not-yet-seen repository whose Python files plus completion file fit 120,000120{,}000 Gemma-3 tokens, until 2020 repositories are collected; the dataset order and commit hashes are recorded, so the selection is deterministic. The context of a repository is the concatenation of its non-empty .py files in snapshot order, each preceded by a header with its path; the completion file itself is not part of the context. The median context is 73,29873{,}298 Qwen tokens (range about 4545k to 9595k). Every listed target line with non-blank content is one question, n=650n=650 in total. A question shows the path of the completion file and its prefix, all lines before the target, in a code fence, and asks for exactly the next line; prefixes longer than 16,00016{,}000 characters are truncated to their tail at a line boundary, which affects two questions. The prefix is part of the question, not of the compacted context, so compaction is tested through the repository context alone. The answer is generated inside an open code fence with at most 6464 new tokens.

Compaction and scoring.

As for LongHealth (Appendix H), each repository is compacted in chunks: consecutive files are packed into chunks of at most 10,00010{,}000 tokens without crossing file boundaries, about nine per repository, each chunk is compacted at the target ratio, and the compacted chunks are concatenated. Head budgets, calibration, final refit, method configurations, and the five-seed protocol are identical to the LongHealth cells; seeds affect calibration-query sampling and generation, not the fixed set of repositories and questions. A completion is correct when its first generated code line, after dropping empty lines and fence lines and stripping surrounding whitespace, matches the reference line exactly; accuracy is the mean over the 650650 questions. Time is query generation plus compaction per repository. The full-context ceiling under the same questions and scorer is 40.6%40.6\%, and the query-free baselines reach 2222 to 23%23\% from the file prefix alone, so the effective range of the benchmark is about 2222 to 4141 points.

Results.

At 100×100\times no calibrated method is more than 0.40.4 points above the best query-free baseline, so the budget rather than the selection rule limits accuracy there. From 50×50\times on, the calibrated methods separate. KV-Surgeon and KV-Surgeon-fast match AM-OMP within uncertainty at 50×50\times with 9.7×9.7\times and 21.5×21.5\times less pipeline time, KV-Surgeon has the highest point estimate at 20×20\times and 10×10\times, and at 5×5\times every calibrated method except KVzip and KVMerger is within 1.81.8 points of the ceiling. OBCache is again the strongest ported method, and AM-OMP-CS is the only prior method within uncertainty of KV-Surgeon at 20×20\times, at 6.7×6.7\times its cost.

Appendix E Component ablations

This section holds every ablation of the shared pipeline and of KV-Surgeon behind Section 4.3 and Table 2: the shared pipeline components in Section E.1, compensation in Section E.2, and the efficiency and design choices in Section E.3. Every ablation runs on Qwen3-4B with QuALITY at 50×50\times, changes one component of the pipeline of Section 3 at a time, and reports the mean over five seeds with one standard error over seeds. Two protocols are used and must not be mixed. The 5050-article protocol (Tables 13 and 15) is that of the main tables, 894894 questions; its self-study controls are the KV-Surgeon, LOO, and AM-HAK entries of Table 1, and its time is pipeline time, calibration-query generation plus compaction. The 2525-article protocol (Table 14) uses the first 2525 articles, so its accuracies are compared only against the reference row of the same panel and never against the main-table numbers, and its time is compaction only, because query generation is identical across arms. The fast-tier row of Table 13 was run with the fast configuration in use at the time of the ablation, whose reference values (65.5%65.5\%, 5.45.4 s) differ from the KV-Surgeon-fast entry of Table 1; it too is read only against its own control. Defaults are those of Appendix C.

E.1 Shared pipeline components: head budgets and final refit

Both components are inherited from attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026) and applied to every calibrated method, so their effect is measured per method. Table 15 switches them independently for our methods and the attention-matching baselines; the ported eviction methods are walked through the same switches in Table 16.

Head budgets. The ablation replaces the optimized per-head budgets of Appendix C by uniform per-layer budgets at the same global ratio. It is the largest single lever, and it is not specific to KV-Surgeon: with the refit in place, KV-Surgeon loses 6.66.6 points, AM-HAK 6.96.9, and LOO 7.87.8. Under uniform budgets KV-Surgeon remains 2.42.4 points ahead of LOO and 3.03.0 ahead of AM-HAK, so the selection-rule margins of Section 4.3 do not depend on the optimized budgets. KVzip, the one baseline that sets its own head allocation from a global attention threshold, leads to the same conclusion: ported with the shared budgets and refit, it collapses under strong compaction, a median of 15.315.3 points below KV-Surgeon-fast at 50×50\times and 100×100\times, yet sits a median of 1.61.6 points below the ceiling at 5×5\times (Appendix D); the deficit tracks how hard the compaction is, not how good the score is.

Final refit. The refit is ablated on the LOO support, where it can be switched off without touching selection (Table 13). Serving the selected keys with their original multipliers and values, which is plain eviction on the score of 13, costs 5.45.4 points against LOO with the refit. Across methods the two switches compound: the budgets are the larger lever, worth +4+4 to +8+8 points on top of the refit, and the refit adds +1+1 to +7+7 on top of raw compaction (Tables 15 and 16). The improvements are not the same for all methods, but KV-Surgeon is ahead in all three settings. Panel (c) of Table 14 decomposes the refit into its two solves on the KV-Surgeon support; it is kept as supporting evidence for Section H.1 and is not built on elsewhere.

E.2 KV-Surgeon-specific component: compensation

Panel (b) of Table 14 isolates compensation. The surrogate, the 4​t4t candidate pool, and the final refit are held fixed and only the compensating update of 12 is disabled, so that elimination proceeds greedily on the same surrogate saliencies. This costs 2.9±0.82.9\pm 0.8 points (seed-paired; 3.03.0 between the seed means of Table 2), and leaves greedy elimination no better than LOO selection on the same articles (64.7%64.7\%). Two controls show that the gain is not a better standalone objective. Greedy elimination on the exact set loss of 4 instead of the surrogate reaches 65.8%65.8\%, 1.1±1.31.1\pm 1.3 below KV-Surgeon and too noisy on 2525 articles to separate from either side. Shrinking the candidate pool to the support itself (pool factor 11 in panel (a)), which leaves the elimination nothing to eliminate or compensate, costs the same 2.92.9 points. The loss-level counterpart, that the compensated support moves toward an exact-refit oracle and that the compensation generalizes to held-out queries, is in Appendix F.

E.3 Efficiency and design choices

The remaining choices change accuracy by at most one standard error at their defaults and mainly control cost.

Mass term. Setting γ0=0\gamma_{0}=0 removes the mass term from the surrogate (Table 13). Accuracy moves by +0.2+0.2 points, within one standard error, at 22 s more pipeline time.

Candidate pool. The elimination runs on the min⁡{T,⌈4​t⌉}\min\{T,\lceil 4t\rceil\} best entries per head by the score of 13 (panel (a) of Table 14). Widening the pool to the full cache changes accuracy by 0.20.2 points (66.966.9 against 66.766.7) and multiplies compaction time by 3.83.8 (1010 against 3838 s); halving it to 2​t2t costs 1.01.0 point.

Mild-compaction fallback. Heads whose budget tt exceeds 30%30\% of their cache are served by plain eviction on the score of 13, without pool, elimination, or final refit: eviction is near-lossless there, the O⁡(t3)O(t^{3}) value solve is the dominant cost and is largest exactly for these heads, and for t>Nt>N the value solve of 23 is underdetermined. Raising the threshold to 1.01.0 disables the fallback (Table 13). The accuracy of KV-Surgeon-fast is unchanged to the reported precision, and its pipeline time rises from 5.45.4 to 7.47.4 s, so the fallback saves 27%27\% of the pipeline. The fallback was not ablated on the self-study tier.

Surrogate refresh. The frozen surrogate can be re-solved at the current normalization ratios μ\mu every 256256 or 6464 eliminations, either reweighting the residuals of 17 (panel (a) of Table 14) or consistently, holding that mass fixed so that the refreshed objective agrees with the served output (panel (b)). At the default pool the reweighted refresh costs 1.61.6 and 1.91.9 points at 1.3×1.3\times and 2.2×2.2\times the compaction time, and the consistent refresh costs 1.3±0.71.3\pm 0.7 and 0.7±0.20.7\pm 0.2 points. Across the pool sweep the refreshed arm is never better than the frozen one beyond one standard error of the difference (the largest apparent gain is +1.0+1.0 at pool factor 11, with standard errors of 1.01.0 and 0.70.7), while its cost grows to 11×11\times at the full cache. At the loss level, measured as in Appendix F, the refresh changes which positions survive, Jaccard 0.550.55 to 0.850.85 against the frozen support, without changing the exact loss after the final refit on calibration or held-out queries (within ±2%\pm 2\% on every head where a refresh occurs). Freezing is therefore kept for cost, not because it regularizes.

Appendix F Compensation at the loss level and calibration robustness

This section measures compensation directly on the attention-output loss rather than through accuracy, and then asks why repeat-pass calibration costs KV-Surgeon less than it costs the exact single-deletion score; Sections 4.3 and 4.4 cite the results. All measurements use Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B, five QuALITY articles, and every head, that is, 14401440 head–article pairs on Qwen3-4B and 12801280 on Llama-3.1-8B. Scores are computed from the self-study calibration queries, and the exact loss of 4 is evaluated on held-out benchmark questions the scores never saw; where the same measurement on the calibration queries differs, it is given in parentheses.

Compensation moves the support toward the oracle and generalizes.

Against an oracle that runs the same greedy backward elimination but scores every candidate deletion by the exact loss 4 after refitting the remaining entries, on the 546546 heads where this is affordable (t≤57t\leq 57, Qwen3-4B), LOO selection sits 46%46\% above the oracle’s loss and KV-Surgeon 25%25\% (median relative loss 0.2130.213, 0.1830.183, and 0.1460.146; random selection 0.2430.243), closing 45%45\% of the gap, and on the typical head the closed fraction is 39%39\%; the oracle is itself greedy, so these gaps are to exact-loss greedy elimination rather than to the optimal support. KV-Surgeon beats LOO on 84%84\% of heads and still shares only 44%44\% of its keys with the oracle set, because many near-equivalent supports exist. On the supports KV-Surgeon selects at 50×50\times, the final refit leaves 25%25\% of the raw-eviction loss on Qwen and 7.5%7.5\% on Llama on held-out questions, against 25%25\% and 7.7%7.7\% on the calibration queries: no head overfits, and on no head is the stored cache worse than eviction. On Llama raw eviction at 50×50\times leaves a loss larger than the output itself, so the final refit, which every calibrated method shares, removes most of the loss there, and selection decides the remainder. The coefficients the elimination itself produces already achieve most of this (31%31\% and 8%8\%), but they cannot be served raw: on 1%1\% of Qwen heads and 5%5\% of Llama heads they exceed the eviction loss, and the final refit never does, which is the loss-level counterpart of the final-refit ablation of Section E.1.

Why repeat-pass calibration costs KV-Surgeon less than the exact score.

Averaged over the eight combinations at 50×50\times, replacing self-study queries with a single repeat pass costs KV-Surgeon 1.21.2 points (Table 1); the drop is 4.34.3 points on LongHealth with Gemma-3-12B and at most 1.31.3 elsewhere. At the level of rankings, recomputing the scores from a single repeat pass drops the Spearman correlation between the surrogate and the exact loss over random deletion sets, computed within one head and one set size, from 0.9050.905 to 0.7860.786 on Qwen and from 0.9290.929 to 0.8330.833 on Llama, and that of the score of 13 from 0.8810.881 to 0.6900.690 on both, so under cheap queries the surrogate loses about half the ranking fidelity the exact score loses. Cross-head comparability, which is what the per-head budget allocation consumes, is unaffected (0.810.81 and 0.910.91 at 98%98\% deletion), so budget allocation does not need self-study queries. The surrogate is therefore less sensitive to the calibration queries than the exact score, not insensitive.

Hypothesis, not tested as a mechanism. The factor (1−Pi​j)−2(1-P_{ij})^{-2} in the exact deletion score amplifies exactly the queries a repeat pass gets wrong: a query for which one token receives unusually large attention contributes disproportionately to that token’s score, so an atypical repeat-pass attention pattern moves the exact ranking more than it moves the frozen surrogate, which contains no such amplification. This is consistent with the measurements above and is a candidate mechanism for the fast-tier robustness of Section 4.4, but it does not establish why AM-HAK degrades more strongly under the same change: AM-HAK ranks tokens by attention mass rather than by either of these objectives, so its larger calibration drop may have a different cause.

Appendix G Ported baselines: from the published regime to ours

H2O, OBCache, KVMerger, and KVzip are serving-time or self-allocating methods; this section describes how each is ported into the offline pipeline. Each port replaces the method’s own queries by the shared repeat-pass calibration queries, keeps its selection score, and serves the selected support with the shared per-head budgets and final refit of Section 3.4. For OBCache, the published observation window of the last 6464 prompt tokens is replaced by the calibration queries, and its second-order score is aggregated over them. Table 16 validates the port by walking each method from its published configuration to our pipeline one component at a time, at 50×50\times on Qwen3-4B with QuALITY under the 5050-article protocol of Appendix C.

The pipeline we use, inherited from Zweiger et al. (2026), is worth 99 to 1919 points to each of the eviction methods we ported to the offline compaction regime; the budgets are the largest single step for KVMerger and KVzip, the refit for H2O, and the calibration queries for OBCache. Even with every component, the best ported rule, OBCache at 62.462.4, stays 3.53.5 points below KV-Surgeon-fast (65.965.9) at the same cost, and H2O at 62.362.3 is within noise of OBCache. The two hybrid configurations with their own queries but our budgets (H2O 58.7±0.258.7\pm 0.2, KVMerger 57.5±0.557.5\pm 0.5) confirm that budgets alone do not close the gap.

Appendix H Cache construction and the role of mass matching

Chunked contexts. Long structured contexts, for example records of several patients, are compacted one chunk at a time. At inference the compacted blocks sit side by side in one cache, and the softmax normalizes across all of them. Block bb therefore competes for the attention of query ii through its total unnormalized mass mib=∑j∈Sbwj​eZi​jm_{i}^{b}=\sum_{j\in S_{b}}w_{j}e^{Z_{ij}}. A compaction that shrinks a block’s mass re-routes attention away from that block and toward its neighbors, even when the reconstruction within the block is perfect. In this setting the absolute mass of a block is meaningful, and it must be preserved alongside the outputs. Lemma 1 makes this precise, and Section H.1 discusses what mass matching can and cannot tell selection.

Lemma 1 (Serving next to other tokens)

Suppose query ii attends to the compacted cache together with further tokens whose unnormalized attention sums to ci​∑ℓ=1TeZi​ℓc_{i}\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}e^{Z_{i\ell}} for some ci≥0c_{i}\geq 0 and whose output on their own is oi′o_{i}^{\prime}. Then the served output is

μi​o^i+ci​oi′μi+ci,compared withoi+ci​oi′1+ci\frac{\mu_{i}\,\widehat{o}_{i}+c_{i}\,o_{i}^{\prime}}{\mu_{i}+c_{i}},\qquad\text{compared with}\qquad\frac{o_{i}+c_{i}\,o_{i}^{\prime}}{1+c_{i}} (24)

for the original cache. The two agree for every ci≥0c_{i}\geq 0 and every oi′o_{i}^{\prime} if and only if o^i=oi\widehat{o}_{i}=o_{i} and μi=1\mu_{i}=1.

Proof. The softmax over all tokens has the denominator ∑j∈Swj​eZi​j+ci​∑ℓeZi​ℓ\sum_{j\in S}w_{j}e^{Z_{ij}}+c_{i}\sum_{\ell}e^{Z_{i\ell}} and the numerator ∑j∈Swj​eZi​j​v^j+ci​oi′​∑ℓeZi​ℓ\sum_{j\in S}w_{j}e^{Z_{ij}}\widehat{v}_{j}+c_{i}o_{i}^{\prime}\sum_{\ell}e^{Z_{i\ell}}. Dividing both by ∑ℓeZi​ℓ\sum_{\ell}e^{Z_{i\ell}} and using ∑j∈Swj​Pi​j=μi\sum_{j\in S}w_{j}P_{ij}=\mu_{i} and ∑j∈Swj​Pi​j​v^j=μi​o^i\sum_{j\in S}w_{j}P_{ij}\widehat{v}_{j}=\mu_{i}\widehat{o}_{i} from 2 and 3 gives the first expression. The original cache is the case S={1,…,T}S=\{1,\ldots,T\}, w=𝟏w=\mathbf{1}, V^=V\widehat{V}=V, for which μi=1\mu_{i}=1 and o^i=oi\widehat{o}_{i}=o_{i}. If o^i=oi\widehat{o}_{i}=o_{i} and μi=1\mu_{i}=1, the two expressions coincide. Conversely, ci=0c_{i}=0 gives o^i=oi\widehat{o}_{i}=o_{i}; then both expressions are convex combinations of oio_{i} and oi′o_{i}^{\prime} with the weights μi/(μi+ci)\mu_{i}/(\mu_{i}+c_{i}) and 1/(1+ci)1/(1+c_{i}) on oio_{i}, which agree for ci>0c_{i}>0 and oi′≠oio_{i}^{\prime}\neq o_{i} only if μi=1\mu_{i}=1. □\square

H.1 The role and limits of mass matching

Attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), the strongest prior offline method, builds its selection and refit around reproducing each query’s attention mass on the compacted block. Two consequences of Section 3.2 matter here: for how the refit must be run, and for what mass matching can tell selection.

Per-position mass fitting is harmful alone and misleading as a selection signal. Non-uniform multipliers change the retained attention pattern, so the original values no longer reconstruct oio_{i} under the reweighted pattern. Fitting multipliers to mass targets without the subsequent value solve is therefore worse than no refit at all, which is why the refit of Section 3.4 applies the two solves only as an ordered unit. This is measured on the KV-Surgeon support: re-solving the multipliers alone scores 12.012.0 points below serving the elimination’s own coefficients with no refit at all, and 14.214.2 below the full final refit (panel (c) of Table 14). The mechanism is the reweighting rather than the mass objective in particular, so the ablation bounds what mass fitting costs when it is run alone and does not separate it from other multiplier objectives. Mass matching also misleads selection. Weighting the mass term heavily, formally γ→∞\gamma\to\infty in 9, reduces the saliency 11 to its mass component, so that entries are ranked by their contribution to reproducing the attention mass alone, as in attention matching, and their values play no role in selection. This discards both factors that the exact loss 13 says matter, the value novelty ‖vj−oi‖2\|v_{j}-o_{i}\|^{2} and the heavy-hitter weight (1−Pi​j)−2(1-P_{ij})^{-2}. At mild compaction the difference is small, because retained masses stay near one and all criteria agree. At aggressive compaction the two criteria part ways, and the exact loss sides with the output: replacing mass ranking by KV-Surgeon selection inside an otherwise identical pipeline is worth 1.31.3 points at 20×20\times, 3.03.0 at 50×50\times, and 4.34.3 at 100×100\times (Figure 2).

None of this contradicts the published attention-matching results, because all of those results combine mass matching with a value refit.

Served multipliers in chunked caches. Lemma 1 says that a compacted block must preserve its attention mass when it is served next to other tokens. We test this on LongHealth with KV-Surgeon-fast on Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, where every context holds five patient records compacted as separate chunks. We vary only what multipliers the compacted entries are served with: the box-constrained refit of Section 3.4, the multipliers that the elimination itself leaves on the support, clamped to the same box, or unit multipliers. Values are refit in all three cases. Each setting is run in two regimes. In the first, all five records are compacted. In the second, two or three records are kept uncompacted next to the compacted ones; the two complementary masks {1,3}\{1,3\} and {0,2,4}\{0,2,4\} are both run, so every record is served once compacted and once uncompacted, and accuracy is split by whether a question asks about a compacted or an uncompacted record.

Three things follow from Table 17. First, unit multipliers are harmless when everything is compacted the same but harmful when compacted cache chunks are served next to uncompacted ones. With all records compacted they cost 1.61.6 and 1.71.7 points. With uncompacted neighbors the same compacted records lose 12.212.2 points at 100×100\times and 8.98.9 at 50×50\times, while the uncompacted neighbors gain 11 to 33 points. This is the re-routing of Lemma 1: a block whose mass falls below the original hands attention to its neighbors. When every block is compacted, the deficits are similar and largely cancel. Second, mass-preserving multipliers make a block’s accuracy independent of its neighbors: for both fitted settings the compacted records score the same whether their neighbors are compacted or not. Third, the multipliers that the elimination leaves on the support, clamped to the box of 22, match the refit within seed noise, so the final multiplier solve can be skipped at no cost. Removing the mass term from the surrogate (γ0=0\gamma_{0}=0) changes every cell within two standard errors, consistent with Section E.3: mass preservation is carried by the served multipliers, not by the selection.

Appendix I Multiplier diagnostics for the unconstrained elimination

Table 18 shows the impact of a relaxation that makes closed-form compensation possible, i.e., relaxing the multiplier coefficients to real numbers instead of positive numbers. Fewer than half a percent of kept coefficients end negative at any ratio, the median head has no negative coefficients, and the numbers are unchanged between the repeat and self-study query tiers. The refit is calibration, not sign repair: it rescales substantially (median relative movement 0.50.5 to 0.80.8, correlation 0.40.4 to 0.70.7) and its pinning at the upper bound grows from 4%4\% of multipliers at 5×5\times to 15%15\% at 100×100\times, where restoring the attention mass requires the largest multipliers. Negative coefficients concentrate in early layers (1–6), and refit movement is largest in late layers (25–34).
